These mechanisms give rise to unique phenomena, including the stabilization of ultra-short double-stranded DNA, the stretching and alignment of single-stranded DNA, the catalytic activity enhancement of ribozymes and DNAzymes, the acceleration of DNA strand reactions, and the efficient construction of DNA-based hybrid nanomaterials and hydrogels. By integrating mechanistic insights with applications, this review highlights the potential of cryogenic strategies in advancing DNA nanotechnology, biophysics, synthetic biology, and nucleic acid data storage. Current challenges and future directions in this rapidly developing field are also discussed.

title: Fluorogenic RNA aptamer-based probes for molecular diagnostics
abstract: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers (FLAPs) activate fluorescence upon binding cognate fluorogens, thereby converting molecular recognition events directly into optical outputs and enabling programmable signal generation for molecular diagnostics. Here, we summarize the core design principles, recent advances, and the key challenges that continue to shape the field. We first categorize nucleic-acid detection strategies by multi-component assembly, split-aptamer, conformational-switching-based probes, and single-nucleotide variant discrimination, which collectively illustrate how FLAP-based probes balance background suppression and signal generation. We then extend this framework to encompass the expanding use of FLAP-based systems beyond nucleic acid detection, where allosteric, reaction-triggered, and transcription-regulated designs have been adapted for sensing chemically diverse non-nucleic acid targets. When integrated with isothermal amplification, particularly through one-pot workflows and in situ FLAP generation during amplification, these systems can directly couple target amplification to signal production in closed-tube formats. Multiplexed detection through spectral encoding, logic-gated, and spatiotemporal readout has further expanded FLAP utility. We also examine progress in intracellular applications, translational deployment, and early validation in real-world sample matrices. Finally, we discuss key considerations for point-of-care and field deployment, including sample pre-treatment, reagent stabilization, and both instrument-based and instrument-free readout formats. More broadly, FLAPs can be viewed as programmable signal-generation modules, whose wider adoption will depend on improved stability, lower background, standardized readout strategies, and reliable performance in complex, real-world environments.

title: Halogen-controlled multi-level oxidation in tetrathiafulvalene-based metal-organic frameworks
abstract: Halogen-induced oxidation provides a direct route to modulate the electronic states of crystalline solids and the associated radical, electronic, magnetic, and host-guest properties, yet structural insight into halogen-dependent redox processes remains unclear. Here we report a tetrathiafulvalene (TTF)-based metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) that undergo halogen-dependent oxidation while retaining single-crystallinity, enabling atomic-level visualization of redox evolution by X-ray crystallography. Exposure to I 2 , Br 2 , and Cl 2 induces progressively higher oxidation levels of the TTF core in MOFs from TTF 0 to TTF ·+ and TTF 2+ , accompanied by the formation of confined halogen counterions including I − 3 , Br − 3 , and Cl species. Magnetic and conductivity measurements, combined with spectroscopic characterization and density functional theory calculations, reveal that redox-state control enables programmable magnetic responses and tunable electrical conductivity, with the TTF ·+ state exhibiting optimal charge transport. This work establishes a general strategy for visualizing and regulating multi-level oxidation in crystalline materials.

title: Multifunctional nucleic acid-based therapy in fibrosis-related diseases
abstract: Fibrosis is a dysregulated tissue repair outcome that potentially affects any organ, contributes to nearly half of deaths in industrialized communities, and exhibits two distinctive features: excessive deposition of extracellular matrix and prolonged inflammation responses. Current therapies for fibrosis remain non-targeted and non-individual methods with limited outcomes, which may result from complex pathological mechanisms. This dilemma highlights the importance of developing advanced therapy to address the above issues. The rapid development of nucleic acid-based therapies, which precisely target various pathological mechanisms, has brought promising prospects for fibrosis treatment, owing to their advantages such as low immunogenicity, easy programmability, effective cellular modulation, and countless therapeutic targets. Irrespective of the demonstrated efficacy of nucleic acids in fibrosis treatment, their vulnerability to circulatory degradation, suboptimal tissue penetration, lack of cellular targeting, poor cellular endocytosis, and limited lysosomal escape ability within cells restricts their successful delivery and attenuates their therapeutic function. To overcome these barriers, researchers have developed diverse nanoparticle platforms, including lipid matrix, polymeric, tetrahedral framework nucleic acid, peptide/protein, and self-modified nanocarriers, all incorporating advanced surface and structural modifications to enhance delivery efficiency. The advanced characteristics of multifunctional nucleic acid-based therapies enable next-generation drug development for fibrosis-related diseases. Therefore, this review systematically categorizes and analyzes these groundbreaking therapies based on their nucleic acid components and delivery systems. Moreover, this review underscores the distinct traits of delivery methodologies in fibrosis and further addresses future perspectives and major challenges of multifunctional nucleic acid-based therapy.

title: Azobenzene-embedded 2D ultrathin polymeric nanosheet-based polymer-inorganic hybrid catalyst for photo-modulated peroxidase-mimetic catalysis
abstract: Stimuli-responsive 2D ultrathin polymeric nanosheets (UTPNSs) are progressively emerged as promising yet underexplored supports to achieve polymer-inorganic hybrid catalysts with tunable catalytic performance and preferable recyclability. Herein, side-chain-typed functional amphiphilic alternating azocopolymers were produced using Ugi multicomponent polycondensation. Subsequent self-assembly was performed to craft micron-scaled 2D lamellar UTPNSs with an ultrathin thickness of ∼3.2 nm, based on the pendant hydrophobic conjugate stacking mechanism. A reversible photo-triggered structural transition from UTPNSs to spherical micelles (∼71 nm) was achieved under alternating UV and visible light irradiation, owing to trans -to- cis photoisomerization of azobenzenes. Furthermore, 2,2-bipyridine-modified UTPNSs were employed as supports to load Pt nanoclusters, yielding polymer-inorganic hybrid nanocomposites. As a proof-of-concept, the catalytic activity of these hybrid nanocatalysts was evaluated toward H 2 O 2 -mediated oxidation of 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine. Notably, UTPNSs-based hybrid nanocatalysts showcased preferable catalytic performance, which was attributable to long-range-ordered ultrathin structure, ultrahigh specific surface area, and preferable hydrophilicity. Repeatable catalytic actions under sequential UV/Visible light irradiations proved the photo-controllable recyclable catalytic performance of the UTPNSs-based hybrid nanocatalysts. Our work presents a feasible strategy for developing stimuli-responsive UTPNSs-based hybrid nanocatalysts with controllable catalytic ability, offering new insights into the rational design of advanced stimuli-responsive catalysts.

title: Trialkyl(aryl)silanes as latent alkyl radical precursors for Giese reactions via photoredox catalysis
abstract: The duality of trialkyl(aryl)silanes renders them valuable and versatile synthons. To date, a number of strategies have been developed to enable aryl transfer from even simple and inert trialkyl(aryl)silanes. However, exploration of alkyl reactivity in general manifold remains challenging, with Fleming-Tamao oxidation practicing as a notable exception. Herein, we report that a mild photoredox catalysis affects exclusive C(sp 3 )–Si bond alkylation of chemically innocuous trialkyl(aryl)silanes. By resembling β-silicon hyperconjugation effect with catalytically generated proximal arene radical cation, we leverage the high stability of silyl cation to drive selective C(sp 3 )–Si bond cleavage, thus unlocking a new strategic concept in prolific use of quaternary organosilane library. Experimental and computational mechanistic studies confirm the attenuation of the C–Si bond with proximal radical cation, revealing positive charge accumulation at silicon during the transition state.

title: Organ-on-a-chip analytical chemistry
Chemical aspects of covalent aptamer development
abstract: Aptamers are synthetic oligonucleotide ligands discovered by in vitro selection, which combine the programmability of nucleic acids with the binding specificity of antibodies. Conventional aptamer-target interactions are noncovalent and based on association-dissociation equilibrium, limiting their robustness in dynamic biological environments. In recent years, “covalent aptamers” have emerged as new molecular recognition modalities that unite the selectivity of aptamer folding with the permanence of chemical covalency. By embedding electrophiles such as N -hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) esters, sulfur fluoride exchange (SuFEx) chemistry, N -acyl sulfonamides (NASA), deoxyoxanosine (dOxa) derivatives, azide-alkyne chemistry and photo-crosslinker into aptamer scaffolds, researchers have realized proximity-enabled and residue-specific bond formation at the target proteins of interest. This review summarizes the recent development and applications of covalent aptamers, with a focus on their electrophile chemistry aspect. We discuss how these electrophiles of covalent aptamers achieve latent and selective reactivity through microenvironment-dependent activation. Building on these chemical principles, we outline the two major development strategies of rational design and in vitro selection, and briefly survey the representative applications, including cell-surface labeling, antiviral activity, and targeted protein degradation. Collectively, these advances position covalent aptamers as an emerging bridge between chemical biology and molecular therapeutics.

title: Crystal phase-dependent performance and reaction pathways of MnO2 for selective oxidation of methane to C2 oxygenates with molecular oxygen
Assembly of dual π-conjugated units toward enhanced birefringence in a 2D organic sulfonate crystal
abstract: Birefringent crystals, which enable precise control and detection of light polarization, are indispensable in advanced laser technologies. However, achieving a birefringence exceeding 0.3 remains a significant challenge. Herein, we report a dual π -conjugated strategy to construct a novel two-dimensional (2D) purely organic sulfonate crystal, (m-AP)(3-pySO 3 ) (denoted as 3PYH; m-AP = m -aminophenol, 3-pySO 3 = 3-pyridinesulfonate), synthesized via a facile solvent evaporation method. 3PYH features a hydrogen-bonded 2D layered architecture assembled from π -conjugated [m-AP] + cations and [3-pySO 3 ] − anions. This crystal exhibits a short ultraviolet (UV) cutoff edge at 271 nm with a wide bandgap of 4.14 eV. Notably, it demonstrates a large visible-region birefringence of 0.36, which is significantly higher than those reported for most 2D sulfates and their derivatives. Combined structural analysis and first-principles calculations reveal that the exceptional birefringence stems from the synergistic enhancement of polarizability anisotropy by dual π -conjugated units, coupled with hydrogen-bond-mediated ordered orientation of aromatic rings, which induces pronounced electron clouds density anisotropy along different directions. This work identifies 3PYH as a promising UV birefringent material and validates the efficacy of the dual π -conjugated strategy for designing sulfonate crystals with strong optical anisotropy.

title: A redox-responsive reversible photoacoustic molecular probe for visualizing atherosclerotic plaque redox status in vivo
abstract: Atherosclerotic plaque stability is closely linked to the local redox status, particularly the imbalance driven by superoxide anion (O •− 2 ). However, non-invasively monitoring the dynamics of superoxide within plaques in vivo and evaluating the modulating effects of anti-inflammatory therapies remains challenging. This study reports a novel redox-responsive reversible photoacoustic probe, ReP, which exhibits reversible and selective photoacoustic signal switching in the near-infrared region in response to O •− 2 and glutathione (GSH). In vitro characterization demonstrated that ReP enables quantitative detection of O •− 2 and GSH with high selectivity under controlled solution conditions. In an atherosclerosis mouse model, ReP successfully visualized the elevated superoxide levels within plaques following systemic inflammatory stimulation. More importantly, this probe could monitor the significant alleviation of plaque redox imbalance after anti-inflammatory treatment with dexamethasone. Collectively, ReP provides a valuable tool for in vivo assessment of plaque redox status and therapeutic efficacy.

title: Redox-adaptive manganese photocatalysis: orchestrating sequential C(sp3)–O and C(sp3)–C(sp3) cleavage with C(sp3)–C(sp3) reassembly
abstract: Manganese photocatalysis has garnered significant attention due to the metal’s natural abundance, low toxicity, and versatile redox behavior. However, the catalytic mode has largely been restricted to classical atom- or electron-transfer pathways. Here, we introduce a novel and operationally simple catalytic system generated via the in-situ assembly of commercially available Mn(OAc) 2 and a phenanthroline ligand upon interaction with the chalcone epoxide substrate. This system integrates three key functions of light-harvesting, redox mediation, and Lewis acid activation within a single manganese complex. This integration enables a sequential metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) and ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) activation process, facilitating the successive cleavage of C(sp 3 )–O and C(sp 3 )–C(sp 3 ) bonds in the chalcone epoxide. The resulting fragments engage in nucleophilic addition to aldehydes or ketones, effecting an efficient formal aryl group exchange to deliver a broad range of β -carbonyl alcohols (80 examples, up to 98% yield). By combining mechanistic innovation, synthetic simplicity, and the multifunctional role of a base metal, this work establishes a distinct and sustainable paradigm for first-row transition metal photocatalysis.

title: Dynamically regulated electron supply within dual-atom Mn sites for enhanced electrocatalytic nitrate conversion into ammonia
abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR) is a promising approach for ambient ammonia (NH 3 ) synthesis and water denitrification. However, its development is hindered by complex multi-proton-electron coupling steps, sluggish kinetics, and undesirable side reactions. Conventional single-atom catalysts (SACs) generally feature a static electronic environment, failing to meet the dynamic electron demands in stepwise reactions and thus impeding further performance improvement in NO 3 RR. Herein, we design a dual-atom Mn catalyst supported on N-doped carbon (Mn 2 -NC) with a Mn 2 N 6 configuration to validate the concept of on-demand electron supply for enhanced NO 3 RR performance. In-situ spectroscopic analysis combined with density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveals that the unique Mn 2 N 6 configuration establishes a tunable electron interaction network between adjacent Mn sites and the N-doped carbon support. This network enables adaptive electron transfer to meet the specific requirements of key intermediates (*NO, *NHO) involved in the rate-determining steps. Benefiting from the dynamically regulated electron supply mechanism, the Mn 2 -NC catalyst exhibits exceptional NO 3 RR performance, achieving an impressive Faradaic efficiency (FE) of ∼93.7% at −0.5 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) (∼75.5% of single-atom Mn catalyst of Mn 1 -NC), and a high NH 3 yield rate of ∼31.5 mg h −1 mg −1 cat. at −0.9 V vs. RHE (∼24.0 mg h −1 mg −1 cat. of Mn 1 -NC). This work establishes a design principle of dynamic electron transfer for multi-step electrocatalysis, offering guidance for developing advanced catalysts for complex redox reactions.

title: Precisely regulated aggregation enables synergistic exciton lifetime and vertical phase separation control for efficient thick-film organic solar cells
abstract: Thick-film (>300 nm) organic solar cells (OSCs) have attracted considerable interest due to their compatibility with roll-to-roll continuous manufacturing technology. However, device performance is bottlenecked by severe donor aggregation, which not only constrains exciton lifetime but also triggers uncontrolled vertical phase separation. Herein, by integrating the advantages of solvent-solute interactions with a layer-by-layer process, we develop a novel strategy using 2,5-dichlorothiophene (DCT) as a guest solvent in chlorobenzene. Using D18 as a model system, we discovered that the characteristically electron-withdrawing sulfur and chlorine substituents in the DCT molecule impart a positive electrostatic potential to the thiophene core. This electronic modulation enables selective interactions between the DCT moiety and the electronegative dithienobenzothiadiazole (DTBT) segments in the D18 backbone with a reinforced dihedral angle. This twisted configuration suppresses excessive aggregation, which can simultaneously elongate exciton lifetime, modulate vertical phase separation, and preserve superior carrier extraction channels. Consequently, the implementation of mixed-solvent engineering yielded a substantial enhancement in photovoltaic performance, with champion values reaching 20.6% (thin-film) and 19.0% (thick-film). By contrast, the chlorobenzene-cast devices exhibited comparatively inferior efficiencies of 19.5% (thin-film) and 13.8% (thick-film). This disparity unequivocally underscores the critical superiority of our solvent engineering approach in preserving high device performance for thick-film devices.

title: Locally excited emission engineering via regioselective spiro-fusion for narrowband red BODIPY emitters with BT.2020 color fidelity
abstract: The development of efficient BT.2020-compliant narrowband red emitters remains an appealing yet challenging task. Herein, we report a site-specific spiro-fusion engineering strategy for BODIPY fluorophores that enables pronounced red-shifting of emission while rigorously maintaining locally excited (LE)-state integrity. Regioselective fusion of two spiro units onto the BODIPY core simultaneously narrows the electronic bandgap and reduces reorganization energy, thereby affording intrinsically narrowband red emission without invoking charge-transfer (CT) states. Spiro fusion at the 1- or 3-position via intramolecular Friedel-Crafts alkylation induces partial CT admixture within the LE state, resulting in inferior emission characteristics, whereas fusion at the 2-position, realized through a challenging oxidative intramolecular dehydrogenation between C(sp 3 )–H/C(sp 2 )–H, preserves a purely LE emissive state. Consequently, the representative emitter 2-SP-MesBF exhibits an emission maximum at 654 nm with an ultranarrow full width at half-maximum (FWHM) of 19 nm (0.055 eV) and a near-unity photoluminescence quantum yield ( Φ PL = 99%). 2-SP-MesBF-based OLEDs deliver outstanding electroluminescence performance, achieving a maximum external quantum efficiency of 21.2% with remarkably suppressed efficiency roll-off, retaining 14.3% even at 10000 cd m −2 . In addition, the devices exhibit high color purity, emitting pure-red electroluminescence with Commission Internationale de l’Éclairage coordinates of (0.712, 0.288), closely approaching the stringent BT.2020 red standard (0.708, 0.292).

title: Light-driven chromism and deformation co-kinetics in an anthracene coordination compound
abstract: Multifunctional integration represents a critical direction for the development of next-generation intelligent materials. For advanced biomimetic intelligent systems, achieving such dual functionality within a single material platform remains a significant design challenge. Herein, we present an anthracene-based crystalline coordination compound [Y 4 (HAc) 2 (OH) 4 (Ac) 7 (NO 3 )]·2H 2 O ( 1 ), which exhibits concurrent photochromism and light-induced deformation under xenon lamp irradiation. These dual responses arise from two distinct but coupled photochemical pathways: stable radical generation and [4+4] photocycloaddition. By integrating compound 1 into a polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) matrix, the resulting soft composite 1-PVA achieves coherent color-morphology dual-mode coordination within an integrated light-controlled platform. This work establishes a strategy for multifunctional integration through light-driven structural dynamics, advancing the development of next-generation biomimetic intelligent systems with coupled camouflage and mobility capabilities.

title: Flexible adsorbents for efficient CO/N2 membrane separation
abstract: The desorption condition is critical for adsorptive applications such as storage and separation, and the usefulness of step-shaped isotherms of flexible adsorbents for enhancing working capacity has been well recognized. Here, we show that this principle is also valid for membrane separation. Targeting the industrially important and challenging CO/N 2 separation application, a pair of isostructural flexible Cu(I)-based adsorbents with contrasting CO isotherm shapes are used as fillers to fabricate mixed-matrix membranes with high separation performances and remarkable stabilities. Moreover, for practical scenarios where neither sweep gas nor vacuum was applied at the permeate side, the adsorbent with a step-shaped isotherm showed up to ca. 90% increase in CO permeability and CO/N 2 selectivity, as compared with those of the counterpart with a conventional Langmuir-type isotherm. These results highlight that the solution-diffusion mechanism for membrane separation should consider the adsorption capacity not only at the feed side but also at the permeate side.

title: Synergistic engineering of squaramide density and substrate accessibility in Zr-MOFs for boosted Friedel-Crafts alkylation
abstract: The development of high-performance hydrogen-bond-donating (HBD) catalysts is hindered by insufficient active site density and poor substrate accessibility in metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). To address this issue, we employed a linker installation strategy to construct squaramide-functionalized Zr-MOFs with scu topology named NKM-506-SQ, PCN-606-SQ and NKM-906-SQ. Among them, NKM-906-SQ demonstrated exceptional performance due to its unique structural advantages. The dual coordination-unsaturated pocket enabled maximum squaramide linker installation, significantly increasing active site density, while the flexible nature of the framework facilitated pore expansion to enhance substrate accessibility. NKM-906-SQ achieved >99% conversion with only 5 mol% catalyst loading while maintaining excellent stability and recyclability in Friedel-Crafts reactions between nitroalkenes and N -methylindole. Moreover, NKM-906-SQ also demonstrated broad substrate scope with high efficiency, particularly for the more challenging N -methylpyrrole. This work provides a strategic approach for optimizing both active site density and substrate accessibility in heterogeneous catalytic systems.

title: Sub-nanochannel induced by interlayer shifting in covalent organic framework membranes enables ultrahigh proton selectivity
abstract: Proton separation is critical for a variety of industrial processes, yet achieving high selectivity for protons over metal ions remains a significant challenge. Here, we report a covalent organic framework (COF) membrane that exhibits exceptional proton-metal ion separation efficiency. The COF membrane features unique sub-nanochannels induced by interlayer shifting, which is achieved via a controlled interfacial polymerization process. These sub-nanochannels provide an optimal size for proton transport while effectively excluding larger metal ions. Additionally, the positive surface charge of the membrane induces electrostatic repulsion toward metal ions and offers abundant hydrogen donors, further enhancing proton transfer. As a result, the membrane exhibited unprecedented selectivity factors for H + /Na + , H + /Sr 2+ , H + /Mg 2+ , H + /Al 3+ , H + /La 3+ , and H + /UO 2+ 2 , with values of 127, 4273, 4738, 1.3 × 10 4 , 1.36 × 10 6 , and 6107, respectively, surpassing most existing membranes by one to three orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical application for the deacidification of highly acidic (3 M HNO 3 ) spent nuclear fuel raffinate, where, within 24 h of continuous operation, the feed acidity decreased by nearly 50%, with no detectable leakage of radioactive metal ions across 30 diverse radioactive cations.

title: Lanthanide control of W–O redox accessibility in atomically precise polyoxometalate clusters for heterogeneous amide hydroboration
abstract: Lanthanides possess distinctive electronic structures and coordination flexibility that make them attractive for catalysis, yet their precise functions in heterogeneous systems remain difficult to resolve because of structural complexity. Atomically precise heterogeneous platforms that allow direct comparison of lanthanide-dependent reactivity are therefore both rare and important. Here we report an isostructural series of atomically precise lanthanidepolyoxometalate (Ln-POM) clusters, [Ln 3 Ni(Sb 4 O 4 )(SbW 9 O 33 ) 3 (NiW 6 O 24 )(WO 2 ) 3 (OAc)(H 2 O) 8 ] 17− ({W 36 Ln 3 Ni 2 }, Ln = Ce, La, Eu), synthesized through a practical one-pot route that can be proportionally scaled up to nearly 10 g per batch for each congener. Among them, {W 36 Ce 3 Ni 2 } serves as an efficient heterogeneous catalyst for the hydroboration of primary and secondary amides with pinacolborane (HBpin), combining tolerance of sensitive functional groups, catalyst recyclability, gram-scale utility, and applicability to the transformation of a structurally complex secondary amide substrate. Importantly, the catalytic trend cannot be explained by simple lanthanide Lewis acidity, but instead tracks the accessibility and persistence of reduced W(V)-enriched states within the W–O framework. Spectroscopic and mechanistic studies indicate that the Ce congener most effectively enables reversible Ce 3+ /Ce 4+ -W 6+ /W 5+ redox coupling, which acts as an electron buffer to promote and sustain catalytically active reduced states. This work thus establishes atomically precise Ln-POM clusters as a platform for understanding how lanthanide identity governs heterogeneous catalytic behavior through framework redox accessibility.

title: Empowering DNA nanotechnology with xeno-nucleic acids
abstract: Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) nanotechnology has unlocked unparalleled precision in bottom-up construction of nanoscale objects and devices, yet the four natural building blocks impose inherent limits on biostability, chemical diversity, and structural adaptability [1].Xeno-nucleic acids (XNAs) are synthetic genetic polymers, typically comprising unnatural sugars (or congeners), non-canonical base pairs, or backbone linkages (Figure 1).XNAs with backbone modifications often exhibit enhanced nuclease resistance and distinct helical properties.In contrast, unnatural base pairs exploit alternative hydrogen-bonding patterns or are stabilized by a combination of shape complementarity, hydrophobic interactions, and packing forces.By integrating XNA motifs into DNA frameworks or replacing the entire backbone, scientists have created hybrid and fully XNA nanostructures with enhanced stability, new morphologies, and tailored biological functions.This Perspective highlights recent breakthroughs in which XNA chemistry meets DNA nanotechnology, focusing on the design principles, structural outcomes, and unique properties imparted by XNA.

title: Modular assembly of tetrahedral units: decoding the atomic blueprint of metal nanomaterials
Single-atom edge site evolution in layered supports: a first-principles investigation
abstract: Layered materials are widely used as supports for single-atom catalysts (SACs); however, most theoretical studies rely on monolayer models with surface-anchored atoms, neglecting interlayer environments under operating conditions. Here, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to investigate 27 transition-metal single-atom (TM 1 ) catalysts supported on an aza-fused π-conjugated microporous polymer (Aza-CMP). All TM 1 catalysts were exclusively coordinated through-layer pores to mimic interlayer environments. Using the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) as a probe, we systematically compared monolayer models (TM 1 /Aza-CMP-ML) with multilayer systems approximated as bilayers (TM 1 /Aza-CMP-BL). In the predicted as-synthesized state, multilayer supports preferentially stabilize interlayer-edge-confined TM 1 -N 4 motifs, whereas monolayers favor pore-edge TM 1 -N 2 coordination. During the catalytic cycle, some TM 1 in the bilayer model interconvert between TM 1 -N 4 and TM 1 -N 2 configurations, leading to interlayer edge oscillations. This dynamic behavior generates distinct active states and reaction pathways, leading to ORR activities generally inaccessible to monolayer models. Notably, the predicted ORR activity of Cu 1 /Aza-CMP-BL, with an onset potential of ∼0.97 V, surpasses that of Pt(111) while maintaining good stability. These results highlight the critical role of interlayer environments and operando dynamics in the rational design of layered SACs.

title: Synergistic Schottky and blackbody effects in Au-Cu2O Janus structures for highly efficient photocatalytic CO2 reduction
abstract: For hybrid photocatalysts, efficient light harvesting and effective charge separation are critical determinants of catalytic performance. In this work, Au-Cu 2 O hybrid structures with blackbody absorption characteristics were synthesized via seeded growth of Cu 2 O crystal domains on blackbody Au seeds. By exploiting ligand-mediated interfacial energy modulation, two representative architectures—Au-Cu 2 O core-shell and Janus-type core-satellite structures—were successfully constructed. Owing to the spatial separation of Au and Cu 2 O domains, the Janus structure exhibits enhanced charge separation through an “electron-sink” effect, leading to superior photocatalytic CO 2 reduction (CO 2 RR) activity compared with its core-shell counterpart. Notably, the Janus Au-Cu 2 O catalyst also shows improved selectivity toward C 2 products, particularly ethane, possibly due to interfacial effects of the Janus architecture that favor CO-CO coupling. This rational structural design and synthetic control strategy offer an effective approach to enhancing photocatalytic efficiency and selectivity, and provide guidance for the development of high-performance photocatalysts.

title: Catalytic enantioselective construction of spiro stereocenters: recent advances and perspectives
abstract: Stereochemically rich, three-dimensional spirocycles not only constitute the core structure of a variety of complex natural products with a broad spectrum of biological activities, but also have been established as a class of privileged chemical space for functional molecules discovery. Particularly, optically active spirocycles are much sought-after in the field of medicinal chemistry, agrochemistry, organic synthesis, catalysis and materials science. Developing efficient methods for facile synthesis of structurally diverse spirocyclic architectures featuring a spiro stereocenter has long been the focus of synthetic chemistry, which is fueled by the drive to “escape from the flatland” in modern drug discovery. With the fast evolution of asymmetric catalysis, the past decade has witnessed remarkable advances in asymmetric catalytic construction of spiro stereocenters, no matter quaternary or tetrasubstituted, as well as other chiral spiro atoms. This review focuses on the synthetic strategies and recent advances in catalytic enantioselective synthesis of spiro stereocenters, and is organized by the type of spiro atoms and then further subdivided according to the types of substrates. The advantages and limitations of each synthetic strategy, as well as the remaining synthetic opportunities, are briefly discussed.

title: Tunable magnetic intercalation superlattices via cation exchange
Tetrahedral framework nucleic acids: a multifunctional DNA nanoplatform for bone and joint disease therapies
abstract: Osteoarticular diseases, including osteoarthritis (OA), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and osteoporosis, represent a significant global health burden characterized by chronic pain and functional impairment. Traditional therapeutic interventions often face challenges such as poor bioavailability, rapid clearance, and systemic side effects. Recently, tetrahedral framework nucleic acids (tFNAs), a class of self-assembled DNA nanostructures, have emerged as a revolutionary platform for osteoarticular therapy. Due to their exceptional biocompatibility, mechanical stability, and high cell internalization efficiency, tFNAs have demonstrated remarkable potential in anti-inflammation, chondroprotection, and promoting osteogenic differentiation. Furthermore, their modular nature allows for the precise delivery of therapeutic payloads, including small molecules and nucleic acid drugs. This review summarizes the structural advantages of tFNAs and their multifaceted applications in various osteoarticular disorders. We also discuss the underlying molecular mechanisms and provide perspectives on the future clinical translation of tFNA-based innovative therapies.

title: Two transition metal borates built from unprecedented {B11} clusters with nonlinear optical properties
abstract: Two transition-metal borates, Na 8 [M{B 11 O 19 (OH)}{BO 2 (OH) 2 }](NO 3 ) [M = Zn ( 1 ), Co ( 2 )] have been made under solvothermal conditions. Compounds 1 and 2 are isostructural and represent the first borate-nitrates constructed from the unprecedented [B 11 O 21 (OH)] 10− clusters. The [B 11 O 21 (OH)] 10− clusters link with [BO 2 (OH) 2 ] 3− units to form one-dimensional chains, which are further linked through MO 4 tetrahedra to form a porous layered framework incorporating seven distinct types of channels. Both compounds crystallize in the acentric space group Pca 2 1 . Second-harmonic generation (SHG) measurements demonstrate that they exhibit moderate nonlinear optical responses, with efficiencies approximately 0.9 and 0.7 times that of KH 2 PO 4 (KDP), respectively.

title: Well tunable iminoboronate chemistry for precise activation energy modulation in vitrimers
abstract: The exchange kinetics of dynamic covalent bonds in covalent adaptable networks (CANs) play a central role in dictating their material properties. However, the limited tunability of conventional single-mode dynamic bond systems has hindered the ability to establish intrinsic correlations between molecular-level bond exchange kinetics and the macroscopic performance of polymer networks. Herein, we engineer iminoboronates with highly tunable exchange activation energies to elucidate the mechanistic role of activation-energy modulation in governing topology and mechanical properties of CANs. By tuning the coupling partners bound to boronic acids, the Lewis acidity of the boron center can be precisely modulated, thereby altering its catalytic effect on imine exchange. When applied to iminoboronate-based vitrimers, this molecular feature affords versatile control over network dynamics and structural stability. Such programmable kinetics not only enables CANs with tunable recyclability, reprocessability, and adhesion under both aqueous and dry conditions, but also allows the direct modulation of temperature-dependent resistivity through relaxation dynamics, underscoring the potential of bond-exchange engineering within multifunctional CANs. This study closely links molecular reactivity with macroscopic performance regulation, providing a theoretical basis and design ideas for the design of vitrimers that are recyclable, processable, and high-performance.

title: Gradient cation-densified structure for robust cobalt-free medium-nickel layered cathodes
abstract: LiNi 0.6 Mn 0.4 O 2 (NM64) is a promising cathode candidate for next-generation lithium-ion batteries owing to its high theoretical capacity and substantially reduced material and manufacturing costs. However, its practical implementation is limited by intrinsically sluggish Li + transport associated with extensive Li/Ni cation disorder and by interfacial parasitic reactions under high-voltage operation. Here we report a gradient cation-densified NM64 via synergistic Al and Mo co-doping, consisting of a thin (∼1 nm) rock-salt surface layer, an ordered cationic subsurface, and a bulk region with suppressed Li/Ni cation disorder. Gradient incorporation of Mo induces a cation-densified surface phase, which mitigates interfacial side reactions and suppresses surface phase reconstruction. Meanwhile, the homogeneous distribution of Al within the bulk lattice significantly reduces Li/Ni cation disorder, thereby enhancing the reaction kinetics. As a result, the synergistic regulation of both surface and bulk structures markedly improves cycling stability and rate capability, while simultaneously affording superior thermal stability, highlighting its strong potential for practical applications.

title: Piezo-assisted mechanochemistry-enabled self-adaptive hydrogels with multimodal mechanical reinforcement
abstract: Natural tissues such as bone and muscle are self-adaptive materials that remodel themselves in response to mechanical forces. Unlike biological systems, synthetic hydrogels fail to adapt to dynamic and complex mechanical environments. Herein, we report a self-adaptive semi-interpenetrating network hydrogel. Its mechanical properties can be enhanced under physiologically relevant stimuli, including shear, compression, and tension. This reinforcement was accomplished via a piezo-assisted mechanochemistry. It enabled in-situ crosslinking polymerization within the hydrogel even under low-intensity mechanical loading. A strain-dependent reinforcement behavior is characterized by a nearly 50-fold increase in the shear storage modulus, a 14-fold increase in the compressive modulus, and a 4-fold increase in the tensile Young’s modulus. The proposed piezoelectrically mediated strategy not only enables in-situ fabrication of hydrogel electrodes with tailored moduli but also improves their interfacial stability and durability for applications in conformal tactile sensors. This work presents a broadly applicable approach for the fabrication of next-generation flexible electronic devices.

title: Achieving 18.47% efficiency in all-small-molecule organic solar cells via a spherically symmetric halogenated adamantane-based additive
abstract: To address the critical challenge of fine-tuning the active layer morphology in all-small-molecule organic solar cells (ASM-OSCs), which limits further enhancement of device power conversion efficiency (PCE), we introduce a morphology control strategy based on a series of spherically symmetric halogenated adamantane additives (1-chloroadamantane (CA), 1-bromoadamantane (BA), and 1-iodoadamantane (IA)). Given its optimal performance among the halogenated adamantanes, the IA additive is subjected to focused analysis to decipher its mechanisms in morphology control and charge-transport improvement. The unique steric hindrance and strong intermolecular interaction of the IA enable precise regulation of film-forming kinetics for donor and acceptor during deposition. This leads to the formation of the active layer morphology featuring highly ordered molecular stacking, appropriate phase separation scale, and reduced defect-state density. Based on this strategy, the devices achieve efficient and balanced charge transport while significantly suppressing non-radiative recombination losses. Ultimately, when processed with the IA additive, the MPhS-C2:N3-based binary ASM-OSC yields a record PCE of 18.47%. This work not only elucidates the critical role of the highly symmetric spherical structure of halogenated adamantane in morphology control but also opens a new direction for its application in organic photovoltaic devices.

title: In-situ activatable DNAzyme sensors for spatially-controlled molecular imaging in living cells
abstract: DNAzyme-based sensors have emerged as valuable tools for biodetection and have contributed significantly to elucidating fundamental physiological mechanisms. Despite remarkable progress, these sensors lack spatiotemporal control and cell selectivity, which limits their application for in situ sensing and imaging within living systems. To address this challenge, in-situ activatable DNAzyme sensors have been developed, enabling controlled molecular imaging with improved spatial precision. In this review, we summarize recent advances in the design of activatable DNAzyme sensors, with a focus on their modular architectures and operational principles. We highlight their representative applications in the spatially resolved imaging of metal ions and RNAs in living cells. Finally, we discuss the current challenges and future directions in this emerging field. We anticipate that this review will inspire the development of next-generation DNAzyme sensors and accelerate their clinical translation for early disease diagnosis, where imaging with high precision and cellular resolution is paramount.

title: Electrocaloric effect in molecular-based ferroelectric materials for future solid-state refrigeration technologies
abstract: Electrocaloric effect (ECE) involves the electric-field-induced change of dipolar order in dielectric materials, which leads to variations of material entropy and temperature, thus showing significant potential in the field of solid-state refrigeration. Among the homogeneous electrocaloric-active (EC-active) materials, molecular ferroelectrics have recently emerged as promising candidates with unique advantages, such as environmental friendliness, structural flexibility, and biocompatibility. In this review, we have summarized the intriguing ECE of some typical molecule-based ferroelectrics, including the fluoropolymers, organic salts, and inorganic-organic hybrids. The structural origin of phase transitions in such molecular ferroelectrics is elucidated, along with the correlation between their phase transitions and EC performances. Given the emergence of fascinating EC properties, the prospects of these molecular ferroelectrics and their development trends in future solid-state refrigeration devices.

title: Programmable DNA nanopores as synthetic transport channels
abstract: DNA nanopores are synthetic channels with programmable geometry, molecular addressability, and modular functionality. Initially developed as single-molecule sensors using ionic current readouts, they are now increasingly engineered for controlled transmembrane transport. We propose to elucidate their design principles based on three core elements. First, body architecture, which determines lumen geometry and physicochemical environment. Second, interface coupling, which controls membrane insertion, orientation, and sealing. Third, functional regulation, which facilitates the dynamic control of transport rate (mass flux), selectivity, and responsiveness. These elements regulate molecular transport across lipid and solid-state interfaces synergistically. Compared with protein and solid-state pores, DNA nanopores enable superior programmable functionalization and modular integration, although ongoing challenges persist in structural stability, electrical noise, and interfacial robustness. We also examine emerging applications in molecular sensing, programmable transport, cell targeting, and confined nanoreactors, before discussing bottlenecks and requirements for design standardization and scalability. These advances have positioned DNA nanopores as a foundation for programmable nanoscale transport and synthetic channel engineering.

title: Light-controlled DNA nanomotors for programmable intracellular transport in synthetic cell-like droplets
abstract: Intracellular transport, essential for cellular function, is driven by biomolecular motors moving along cytoskeletal networks. While in vitro models have advanced our understanding, replicating the versatility and controllability of native intracellular transport remains challenging. Here, we report a synthetic cell-like model equipped with a light-controlled DNA-based motor capable of light-guided transport along an artificial DNA cytoskeleton. The system consists of self-assembled DNA fibers serving as structural scaffolds and RNA hairpins functionalized with a photocleavable linker (PC-linker) as motor tracks. Upon UV (ultraviolet) irradiation, the motors conjugated to SUV (small unilamellar vesicle) or nanoparticles are activated via strand displacement and RNase H-mediated hydrolysis, enabling directional motion along the fiber axis. Encapsulated within water-in-oil emulsion droplets to mimic cellular confinement, these synthetic cell-like droplets allow spatiotemporally controlled SUV transport using light. This programmable and biocompatible platform offers a robust model for studying subcellular dynamics and paves the way for advanced synthetic biology applications.

title: Dynamic nucleic acid assembly at the cell membrane interface: from spatial biomarker profiling to cellular functional regulation
abstract: Dynamic nucleic acid assembly at the cell membrane interface has emerged as a powerful strategy for engineering programmable biointerfaces capable of molecular sensing, signal processing, and functional regulation. This review summarizes recent advances in membrane-confined dynamic DNA assemblies and their applications in both spatial biomarker profiling and functional reprogramming of cellular behaviors. By integrating programmable DNA nanostructures with molecular recognition elements and nucleic acid reaction circuits, membrane-anchored DNA assemblies enable highly sensitive and multiplexed imaging of cell-surface biomarkers, including membrane proteins, glycosylation patterns, and receptor interactions, thereby facilitating precise identification of diseased cells. Beyond molecular sensing, dynamic DNA frameworks assembled on both the outer and inner leaflets of the plasma membrane provide new strategies for regulating cellular functions through controlled receptor clustering, intracellular signaling modulation, and programmable cell-cell interactions. The review also addresses key challenges and outlines future directions for adaptive nucleic acid biointerfaces in precision diagnostics, therapeutic regulation, and synthetic cell engineering.

title: Trifluoromethylthio-modulated cyanocarbene for diastereoselective cyclopropanation and broad-scope Doyle-Kirmse reactions
abstract: Trifluoromethylthio-substituted hypervalent iodine precursor ( SCF 3 - EBX ) was developed for the efficient in situ generation of trifluoromethylthio cyanocarbene upon reaction with TMSN 3 . The SCF 3 group plays a dual role: its strong electron-withdrawing inductive effect maintains high carbene electrophilicity, while sulfur lone-pair conjugation stabilizes the singlet ground state via a large singlet-triplet gap (Δ G = 14.6 kcal/mol). This unique electronic modulation enables the carbene to achieve an unprecedented balance between reactivity and selectivity under mild, metal-free conditions. It facilitates highly diastereoselective [2+1] cyclopropanation of styrenes (dr > 85:15) and, notably, enables Doyle-Kirmse reactions with allylic, propargylic, allenic, and homoallenic sulfides— transformations previously challenging for triplet-dominated cyanocarbenes. The system exhibits broad functional group tolerance and gram-scale applicability. Comparative experiments and DFT calculations confirm that SCF 3 substitution substantially lowers the barrier for carbene generation and suppresses triplet side pathways. This work not only presents a cyanocarbene system that achieves both high activity and selectivity, but also establishes a general strategy for modulating carbene electronic structure through rational substituent design.

title: The critical role of pH-dependent interfacial water-Pt interaction in hydrogen oxidation reaction
GalNAc-modified triangular DNA origami enables liver-directed delivery of gossypol acetate for APE1-targeted therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains difficult to treat because of limited drug selectivity, insufficient intracellular delivery, and persistent resistance supported by efficient DNA repair. To address these limitations, we developed an N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-engineered triangular DNA origami nanoplatform for liver-directed delivery of gossypol acetate (GAA) in HCC. Mechanistically, GAA directly inhibited the endonuclease activity of APE1, with an IC 50 of 8.472 µM. The Origami-GalNAc-GAA formulation showed acceptable in vitro cytocompatibility and hemocompatibility and enhanced cellular internalization in Hepa1-6 cells. Compared with free GAA or nontargeted Origami-GAA, Origami-GalNAc-GAA more effectively suppressed proliferation, clonogenicity, migration, and proangiogenic phenotypes while promoting oxidative stress-associated apoptosis. These enhanced antitumor effects were accompanied by increased DNA damage, elevated γH2AX and Chk2 signaling, and reduced XRCC1 expression, indicating the amplification of DNA damage responses together with the attenuation of repair-related signaling. In an orthotopic Hepa1-6 liver tumor model, Origami-GalNAc-GAA enhanced liver-associated accumulation and improved antitumor efficacy in vivo . In summary, this work establishes a programmable GalNAc-functionalized DNA origami platform for liver-directed delivery of an APE1-targeting small molecule and provides a rational nanomedicine strategy for improving DNA repair-targeted therapy in HCC.

title: DNA-mediated carbon nanotube sorting: progress, mechanisms, and perspectives
Antisite-disorder-tailored anisotropic negative thermal expansion and synergistic multifunction in Mn2CuReO6
abstract: While antisite disorder (ASD) typically serves as a detrimental defect in materials, the interplay between ASD, atomic site splitting, and multifunctional coupling in polar oxide systems has not been fully elucidated, limiting the rational design of ASD-tailored functional materials. Herein, we demonstrate that ASD can act as an effective functional design parameter in the new polar oxide Mn 2 CuReO 6 , synthesized via a high-pressure and high-temperature route. Combined characterizations, including neutron/synchrotron X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and first-principles calculations, reveal that significant Mn/Cu ASD tailors two distinct macroscopic properties by inducing a graded, site-specific off-center displacement of A-site cations. First, a low-energy dielectric relaxation originates from the reorientation of local dipoles at the Mn1 site. Second, a pronounced negative thermal expansion along the c-axis in the temperature range of 5–70 K is mediated by a magneto-lattice coupling mechanism that is fundamentally distinct from conventional models such as rigid unit modes or magnetovolume effects. Our results demonstrate that ASD-tailored local lattice flexibility constitutes the common foundation of these multifunctional responses, and thereby establishes ASD as a powerful design strategy for the synergistic control of magnetic, thermal, and dielectric behaviors.

title: DNA nanotechnology as a programmable precision interface for quantum control and devices
abstract: Quantum technologies increasingly require deterministic control over nanoscale geometry, because light-matter coupling, spin-dependent transport, excitonic interactions, and electronic device performance are highly sensitive to distance, orientation, chirality, and collective organization. Conventional top-down fabrication and non-DNA self-assembly strategies have enabled substantial progress in nanophotonic, spintronic, and electronic systems, yet they often remain limited in simultaneously achieving molecular-scale addressability, three-dimensional programmability, and site-specific heterogeneous integration. DNA nanotechnology offers a complementary bottom-up strategy by translating sequence information into programmable spatial coordinates, allowing functional components to be positioned, oriented, and organized with nanometer-scale precision and, in selected DNA mechanical systems, sub-nanometer designed displacement control. In this Review, we discuss DNA nanotechnology as a programmable interface for quantum-relevant control and device integration. We first summarize the spatial degrees of freedom that govern nanoscale interactions, including orientation, distance, topology/chirality, and collective organization. We then examine how DNA origami, DNA bricks, curved and twisted frameworks, and surface-registered DNA architectures enable structural programming across molecular, nanoscale, and device-relevant length scales. We further review DNA-enabled spin-selective transport and programmable spin-density patterning, DNA-templated assembly of nanodiamonds, quantum dots, plasmonic nanoparticles, and one-dimensional electronic channels such as carbon nanotubes, as well as recent efforts to integrate DNA-defined structures with photonic cavities, plasmonic waveguides, two-dimensional materials, and electronic devices. Finally, we discuss key challenges related to environmental stability, interfacial cleanliness, assembly fidelity, component heterogeneity, chip-level registration, and structure-function validation. Rather than replacing conventional nanofabrication, DNA nanotechnology provides a molecularly precise interface for encoding geometry into functional quantum-relevant architectures, offering a promising route toward scalable quantum optoelectronics, programmable spin interfaces, and bio-integrated quantum sensing platforms.

title: Defect-trapping multiphoton-mediated upconversion nanoprobes enabling super-resolution imaging
Activating out-of-plane carrier transport in two-dimensional polymers for efficient photocatalytic overall water splitting
Enantioselective collective synthesis of chiral helicenes via covalent organocatalytic kinetic resolution
abstract: Chiral helicenes are widely utilized in the research fields of materials science, molecular self-assembly, and asymmetric catalysis. However, the asymmetric synthesis of helical scaffolds remains a substantial challenge, especially when compared to the well-developed synthetic protocols for other types of chiral frameworks. The main obstacles include the limited availability of suitable starting materials and the lack of catalytic systems capable of effectively controlling the helical stereochemistry. Herein, we report an unprecedented collective synthesis of a new class of helicene quinones ranging from [5] to [7] through an enantioselective [4+2] annulation. This method features a broad substrate scope, excellent functional-group tolerance, and rapid access to diverse helicene quinones with good yields and high enantioselectivities. Furthermore, the optical properties of synthetic compounds were characterized, revealing their promising potential for applications in material sciences.

title: Self-pressurizing nanoreactors for selective electrocatalysis
High-mobility emissive organic semiconductors towards organic light-emitting transistors
abstract: High mobility emissive organic semiconductors (HMEOSCs) represent a unique class of materials that combine efficient charge carrier mobility with strong solid-state emission. Such an important multifunctional material system holds great potential for applications in various optoelectronic devices, especially organic light-emitting transistors (OLETs). However, the development of HMEOSCs has been challenged due to the long-term scientific bottleneck of the molecular structures and packing modes of semiconductor materials that are capable of simultaneously exhibiting high charge carrier mobility and strong solid-state emission. Encouragingly, there are significant advances in HMEOSCs through rational molecule design and other multi-component doping and cocrystal strategies, which not only improve the performance and functions of existing organic optoelectronic devices but also open up new avenues for device applications. In this review, we present a timely overview of these exciting advances in HMEOSCs and discuss their promising applications with some representative examples reported so far. Furthermore, a conclusion and some guiding significance for potential future development in this field are provided, such as spin OLETs and electrically pumped organic lasers. Hopefully, there will be a rapid development and bright future for HMEOSCs and their applications under the joint efforts of scientists from different fields.

title: Plasmonic nanoantenna sensor for ultrasensitive ozone detection with single-particle visualization
abstract: Ozone exposure has emerged as a growing global health concern. Traditional techniques rely on bulky instrumentation, stringent operating conditions, and limited sensitivity, restricting their applicability for real-time and decentralized monitoring. Here, we report a facile yet highly efficient plasmonic nanoantenna sensor (PNOS) that enables direct visual readout of ozone exposure. The sensor is fabricated through electrostatic assembly of 75-nm silver nanocubes onto positively charged SiO 2 /Si substrates, using polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) as a negatively charged end-capping ligand on the surface of the silver particles. First-principles calculations reveal that, in contrast to conventional ligands (e.g., SH-PEG-NH 2 , SH-PEG-COOH), PVP enables efficient ionic accessibility. Upon O 3 exposure, the reaction and removal of PVP by O 3 induce oxidative conversion of interfacial silver nanocubes into Ag 2 O and uncover AgCl domains, inducing pronounced red-shifts in dark-field scattering spectra. Significantly, the PNOS chip demonstrates an ultralow detection limit of 8 ppb for O 3 , outperforming that of previously reported optical sensors. This ligand-gated and irreversible surface transformation yields visually interpretable plasmonic responses with exceptional sensitivity, establishing a single-use optical dosimetric platform for ozone exposure in atmospheric settings and for oxidative-species-responsive readout in biological contexts.

title: Luminescent-reaction-enabled super-resolution microscopy: from structure to biochemical activity
Rare-earth complexes: an aspect of radical-related reactivity
abstract: The highly reactive organic radicals play indispensable roles in a vast range of fields, including synthetic chemistry, biochemistry, polymer chemistry, and environmental science. However, the high reactivity and inherent instability of organic radicals pose significant challenges in their synthesis, isolation, and reactivity manipulation. Since the early 1990s, metalloradicals, which have tunable structures and reactivities, have emerged as a promising alternative to organic radicals and have been applied in many important chemical processes, such as catalysis (metalloradical catalysis, MRC) and living radical polymerization. In comparison, the rare-earth complex has been more of a spectator in those research fields until lately. In particular, with the most stable and commonly seen formal oxidation state, RE(III) ions, except for Sc(III), Y(III), La(III), and Lu(III), feature open-shell electronic structures with the [Xe]4 f 0–14 electron configuration. However, the reported reactivities of those RE(III) complexes are usually regulated by their Lewis acidity. Recently, the radical-like reactivity of rare-earth complexes has been gradually unveiled. With a focus on radical-related processes and reactivities, this review summarizes the metal- and ligand-centered redox processes of rare-earth complexes, the reactivity of rare-earth complexes with unconventional oxidation states, and the stoichiometric and catalytic radical-based transformations mediated by rare-earth complexes.

title: Progress in coinage metal-based electrocatalysts for nitrate reduction reaction
abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR), which can convert nitrate into harmless nitrogen gas or valuable products including ammonia and carbon-nitrogen coupled chemicals under mild conditions, is considered a promising strategy for both pollution control and resource recovery. Electrocatalysts based on coinage metals (copper, silver, and gold) demonstrate significant advantages in this process. Their unique capability to adsorb and activate nitrogen-containing intermediates, coupled with their tunable electronic structures, underpins their effectiveness. This review systematically summarizes recent progress in the application of coinage metal-based electrocatalysts for the NO 3 RR. It focuses particularly on elucidating the underlying reaction mechanisms and on pathways for steering the conversion of nitrate towards N 2 , NH 3 , and C–N coupled products. The structure-property relationships of these catalysts are discussed in depth. Strategies including alloying, facet engineering, defect control, interface design, and local microenvironment optimization have been shown to effectively enhance the activity, selectivity, and stability of the catalysts. Furthermore, the review outlines the main challenges currently faced in this field. Finally, future research directions are proposed. This work aims to provide guidance for designing efficient and stable coinage metal-based electrocatalysts for nitrate conversion and to promote sustainable development in areas such as wastewater treatment, nitrogen resource recovery, and green synthesis.

title: Linker dimensionality extension-induced topological evolution in MOFs for boosting methanol-to-olefin product separation
abstract: Precisely controlling the pore architecture of porous materials is crucial for boosting adsorptive separations, yet achieving fundamental pore reconfiguration beyond incremental tuning remains highly challenging. Herein, we introduce a “linker dimensionality extension” strategy to deliberately steer the topological evolution of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), thereby enabling a profound reconstruction of pore geometry. The stepwise increase in linker dimensionality from two-dimensional (2D) (BDC 2− ) and quasi-3D (CYHDC 2− ) to 3D (BODC 2− ) triggered a directional change in Cu 2 paddlewheel nodes, transforming the topology from a 2D square lattice ( sql ) into a 3D niobium oxide ( nbo ) net and the pore structure from 1D channels to 3D interconnected cages in a new Cu(II)-MOF (CTGU-48). The cage-type pore environment, coupled with high densities of open metal sites and alkyl groups, endows CTGU-48 with impressive separation properties toward methanol to olefins (MTO) products: high C 3 H 6 uptake (170 cm −3 g −1 ), selectivities for C 3 H 6 /C 2 H 4 (9.6) and C 2 H 6 /C 2 H 4 (C 2 H 6 -selective: 1.9) at 298 K, and C 2 H 4 productivities (0.31–157.7 L kg −1 , ⩾ 99%, 298 K) in binary mixture separation processes under diverse conditions. Its outstanding performance arises from the synergy and balance between thermodynamic affinity and kinetic diffusion, as confirmed by both experimental and theoretical studies. By demonstrating that linker dimensionality can act as a powerful structural-directing factor via topological intervention, this work provides a new vision for constructing advanced pore structures for challenging separations.

title: Revisiting lithium dendrite mechanics
Engineering hollow covalent organosulfur nanocomposites for stable and high-rate Na/K-S battery cathodes
abstract: Room-temperature Na/K-S batteries have shown great promise as high-energy-density and cost-effective energy storage devices. However, building cathodes for Na/K batteries is much more challenging than that for Li-S batteries, mainly due to the much more sluggish redox conversion kinetics together with much larger volumetric deformation and serious soluble polysulfide shuttling. The existing routes for building high-performance sulfur cathodes usually suffer from multi-step and intricate processes that hinder scalability. Herein, we report that the structural engineering of sulfur species into hollow covalent organosulfur (HCOS) nanocomposites demonstrated high conceptual and technological potential for stable high-rate cathodes for both Na/K batteries. Such HCOS nanocomposites could be facilely fabricated via a very simple one-step pyrolysis with a small organic molecule (e.g., 1,4,5,8-naphthalenetetracarboxylic dianhydride) and elemental sulfur (S 8 ). The covalently bonded sulfur (44.8 wt%), which was highly dispersed within the carbon matrix, exhibited superior redox reactivity and enabled a fast and shuttle-free conversion reaction. The hollow nanostructure with a thin nanoscale shell and built-in cavities effectively reduces the charge transfer distance and buffers the volume deformation. As cathodes for Na-S and K-S batteries, the resultant HCOS cathode demonstrates a combination of outstanding cyclability (e.g., ∼100% capacity retention after 2000 cycles for Na-S batteries), promising capacity, and high-rate capability. Our findings opened a new avenue for building functional sulfur cathodes toward stable high-rate Na/K-S batteries.

title: Deciphering molecular design for MR-TADF emitters based on attenuated charge-transfer frameworks
abstract: Incorporating hole-transport moieties (HTMs) into narrowband boron-nitrogen multiple-resonance (BN-MR) frameworks often leads to unwanted dual emission and broadened spectra, compromising color purity. We present a design strategy that combines a rigid, high-energy indolocarbazole (InCz) weak donor with sterically diverse BN-embedded polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (BN-PAH) acceptors. A series of emitters featuring weak long-range charge-transfer character and tunable emission properties was synthesized. The BN-PAH unit not only exhibits narrowband emission but also imposes strong steric hindrance, suppressing intramolecular rotation, enabling anti-Kasha emission with a notably narrowband emission. The InCz unit, with its “waterfall-like” energy gradient, also serves as a hole-transport component and a partial host, thereby boosting device performance. In dilute toluene, the emitters show ultranarrow photoluminescence with full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) values of 17–20 nm, even narrower than the parent BN-PAHs. OLEDs based on InCz- t CzIBN achieve a maximum external quantum efficiency of 39.1% with an electroluminescence FWHM of ∼23 nm, ranking among the best-performing green MR-TADF devices. This work offers a versatile strategy for efficient, color-pure emitters for ultra-high-definition displays.

title: A zeolite-confined Ni catalyst overcoming the pyridine poisoning dilemma
Molecular skeleton programming enables advanced lithium-sulfur batteries
Narrowband green electroluminescent emitters with low-driving voltage, robust power efficiency, and stability
abstract: Achieving operational stability, high efficiency, low operating voltage, and narrow-band electroluminescence in green emitters remains a fundamental challenge in organic light-emitting diode (OLED) technology. This work introduces three novel single-boron/nitrogen (B/N) core multiple-resonance thermally activated delayed fluorescence (MR-TADF) emitters, SNBN, SOBN, and SFBN—designed by modular substitution of naphthalene, dibenzothiophene (DTP), dibenzofuran (DF), or dimethylbenzofluorene (DMBF) units into the B/N core. These emitters exhibit green emission peaks between 501 and 522 nm, with exceptionally narrow full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) values of 21–23 nm, attributed to suppressed molecular vibrations enabled by the modular substituents. Additionally, they demonstrate high photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQYs) exceeding 90%. In optimized ternary phosphorescent host-sensitized OLEDs, devices based on SNBN achieve an extremely low driving voltage and a remarkable power efficiency of approximately 150 lm/W. The SNBN-based device also shows an operational lifetime ( T 50 ) of 357.1 h at a constant current density of 10 mA/cm 2 . The enhanced molecular stability imparted by the naphthalene substitution in SNBN underpins this outstanding performance, positioning it as a promising candidate for next-generation green emitters in portable electronics ( e.g. , smartphones) and augmented/virtual reality (AR/VR) displays.

title: Cooperative non-covalent interactions for low-temperature PET upcycling
Construction of highly efficient liquid-ionic fluorescent polymeric probes by regulating anion charge density
abstract: We demonstrate a strategy for constructing highly efficient fluorescent probes by modulating the anion charge density, using picric acid (PA) as a detection model. An imidazolium-capped poly(diphenylacetylene) is combined with six anions of decreasing charge density (BF − 4 , PF − 6 , FSI − , Tf 2 N − , Pf 2 N − , Nf 2 N − ) to detect PA and other nitroaromatic explosives. Fluorescence quenching measurements show a monotonic increase in sensitivity as anion charge density decreases. The highest Stern-Volmer constant ( K sv = 2.38 × 10 5 M −1 ) and lowest limit of detection (LOD = 63 nM) were observed for the PIMI-Nf 2 N system. Photo-luminescence quenching analysis indicates predominantly dynamic quenching in all six polymer-PA systems, with an additional static component for the Pf 2 N − and Nf 2 N − variants. Both photoinduced charge transfer and fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) processes contribute to the quenching. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that lower charge-density anions have reduced energetic barriers for exchange with the PA anion, reflecting weaker binding to imidazolium and facilitating ion exchange. Lower anion charge density also allows PA to approach the fluorescent moiety more closely, enhancing energy and charge transfer. PIMI-Nf2N exhibits excellent selectivity for PA over other nitroaromatic analytes. This study elucidates how counter-anion structure influences PA sensing performance and suggests a strategy for designing ionic-liquid-based fluorescent probes.

title: Regulating the local aromaticity of solid additives to enhance intermolecular interactions and realize 20%-efficiency organic solar cells
abstract: The improvement of organic solar cells (OSCs) efficiency urgently requires precise control of the morphology of the active layer. Traditional additive design has largely focused on halogenation or isomerization strategies, while the local aromaticity (LA) of molecules has not yet attracted attention. In principle, the LA of a molecule is a key parameter for governing electron distribution and intermolecular interactions. Herein, we propose a strategy to enhance interactions with photoactive materials by finely tuning the LA of solid additives. We utilized acenaphthylene (ACY) and acenaphthene (AP) as model additives, which share an identical skeleton but differ in aromaticity. The theoretical calculations reveal that AP exhibits enhanced local aromaticity in its naphthalene ring due to the saturated five-membered ring, leading to more localized electron clouds, a stronger electrostatic potential gradient, and a larger dipole moment. Consequently, AP forms stronger electrostatic and van der Waals interactions with the donor D18 and the acceptor L8-BO. Experimentally, AP effectively promotes ordered molecular packing, improves crystallinity, and optimizes blend morphology, enabling a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 19.58% in D18:L8-BO-based devices. Moreover, devices based on AP optimization exhibit improved stability. Notably, combined with layer-by-layer processing and a 1,4-diiodobenzene (DIB) additive, the efficiency is further boosted to 20.09%. The additive also demonstrates broad applicability across multiple photovoltaic systems. This work establishes “local aromaticity tuning” as a novel design strategy for solid additives, providing a new direction for the development of high-performance OSCs.

title: Engineering asymmetric single copper atoms for scalable ammonia electrosynthesis
Homogenized interfacial physical field for stable zinc metal anodes
abstract: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) are promising energy storage systems due to their safety and low cost. However, zinc metal anodes (ZMAs) suffer from dendrite growth, hydrogen evolution reaction, and corrosion parasitic reactions, leading to capacity decay and performance deterioration. To address these issues, a uniform and dense two-dimensional planar conjugated zinc-squaric acid metal–organic coordination compound (denoted as ZnSQ) was in-situ constructed on the surface of ZMAs via a spatially confined self-assembly approach between squaric acid (SQ) and ZMAs. Benefit by the unique π-conjugation characteristics of the ZnSQ-based interfacial layer, the electric field and Zn 2+ flux are distributed uniformly, which facilitates uniform Zn 2+ migration, plating and stripping, further suppresses dendrite growth and parasitic reaction formation. Symmetric cells of the modified ZMAs exhibit excellent long-term cyclability (4600 h) and high coulombic efficiency at 4 mA cm −2 and 1 mA h cm −2 , while full cell maintain high capacity retention even under high current densities (78.5% at 5 A g −1 ). This work presents a simple and effective strategy for addressing dendrite and corrosion problems in ZMAs through the design of a π-conjugated two-dimensional interfacial layer, further improving AZIBs cycling life and reversibility for better zinc-based energy storage devices.

title: Encapsulation-regulated oxygen affinity at Ni-CeO2 interfaces for ethanol steam reforming
abstract: Engineering metal-oxide interfaces to regulate the reactivity of oxygen-containing species is central to heterogeneous catalysis. Herein, we report a mesoporous CeO 2 -encapsulated Ni catalyst (Ni@ m -CeO 2 ) for hydrogen production via ethanol steam reforming (ESR) and compare it with a non-encapsulated analogue supported on the same mesoporous CeO 2 framework (Ni/ m -CeO 2 ). Encapsulation confines Ni nanoparticles beneath a mesoporous CeO 2 overlayer without sacrificing reactant accessibility, thereby creating a distinct Ni-CeO 2 interfacial environment with stronger metal-support interaction and a higher concentration of oxygen vacancies. As a result, Ni@ m -CeO 2 exhibits enhanced ESR activity, stability, and selectivity toward CO 2 and H 2 , and sustains near-complete ethanol conversion for 100 h without measurable deactivation under high-pressure conditions. In situ spectroscopy, probe-reaction analysis, kinetic analysis, and oxygen-affinity measurements collectively support a common acetate-mediated ESR pathway on both catalysts, while revealing that encapsulation weakens the binding of oxygen species at Ni sites and increases the apparent reactivity of interfacial hydroxyl species. A volcano-type dependence on Ni particle size further shows that catalytic performance is governed by both the availability and the chemical state of Ni-CeO 2 interfacial sites. These results identify oxygen affinity on the Ni side as a key descriptor governing interfacial OH* reactivity at Ni-CeO 2 boundaries, offering a general strategy for designing efficient non-noble metal catalysts for reforming reactions.

title: Mechanistic understanding and catalyst design principles for CO2, CO, and CO2/CO mixed-feed methanation
abstract: Methanation of carbon oxides, including CO 2 , CO, and their mixtures, is important for renewable energy storage and synthetic natural gas production. CO 2 hydrogenation generally follows associative formate-related pathways, whereas CO methanation mainly involves dissociative adsorption and C–O bond cleavage, requiring different catalyst functions. These mechanistic differences emphasize the roles of interfacial engineering, oxygen-vacancy regulation, and metal-support interactions in improving activity, CH 4 selectivity, and stability. In CO 2 /CO mixed feeds, methanation is controlled by competitive adsorption, temperature-dependent surface coverages, and coupling between \({\rm CO}_{2^{-}}\) and CO-derived hydrogenation pathways. Strategies such as rare-earth doping, inverse oxide-metal architectures, tandem active sites, and electronic promoters enhance CH 4 formation by coordinating CO activation, CO 2 adsorption, hydrogen spillover, and interfacial intermediate transfer. This review further identifies five transferable design principles: site-function partitioning, adsorption-strength balance, interfacial electronic regulation, vacancy/basic-site management, and architecture-controlled pathway coupling. These principles provide a unified structure-performance framework for rational catalyst design under CO 2 , CO, and mixed CO 2 /CO methanation conditions.

title: Anionic environment engineering in metal oxides accelerates water electrolysis
abstract: The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) involves a complex four-electron transfer process with sluggish kinetics, requiring efficient and stable OER catalysts. Metal oxides have demonstrated significant potential for the OER, with increasingly diverse strategies for performance optimization. By precisely controlling the anionic composition of materials, their electronic structure, lattice characteristics, and surface microenvironment can be effectively modified, thereby substantially enhancing their catalytic activity and stability. However, a systematic review of anionic regulation strategies for metal oxide OER catalysts is still lacking. This review addresses this gap by comprehensively integrating recent advances and proposing a unified anionic environment engineering framework encompassing lattice environment regulation, surface environment regulation, and electrolyte environment regulation. It further examines advanced in-situ characterization techniques and theoretical computational methods used to elucidate the underlying mechanisms. The application potential and challenges of this approach in complex systems, such as seawater electrolysis, are discussed. Finally, future research directions are outlined, including the in-situ tracking of reaction dynamics, the exploration of synergistic multi-anion effects, and the development of data-driven design methodologies.

title: Non-fluorinated liquid electrolytes for lithium batteries
Morphological biomimetics of luminescent organisms enabled by stimuli-responsive dual-fluorescent hydrogel-based modular robots
abstract: Biomimetics has promoted technological breakthroughs in many fields like biomedicine and materials engineering.
